# Instructions

Given an input text output it transposed.

Roughly explained, the transpose of a matrix:

```text
ABC
DEF
```

is given by:

```text
AD
BE
CF
```

Rows become columns and columns become rows.
See [transpose][].

If the input has rows of different lengths, this is to be solved as follows:

- Pad to the left with spaces.
- Don't pad to the right.

Therefore, transposing this matrix:

```text
ABC
DE
```

results in:

```text
AD
BE
C
```

And transposing:

```text
AB
DEF
```

results in:

```text
AD
BE
 F
```

In general, all characters from the input should also be present in the transposed output.
That means that if a column in the input text contains only spaces on its bottom-most row(s), the corresponding output row should contain the spaces in its right-most column(s).

[transpose]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpose


Implement the existing API. Use only the standard library. Do not change tests or build manifests. Original tests are available in the workspace.
Run all tests with `python3 -m unittest discover -p '*_test.py'`.


Additional verification workflow:
Before editing, inspect the relevant code and run existing tests. Identify a small
reproduction or acceptance check. Make the smallest correct change. Exercise edge
cases, rerun the original tests, and review the diff for unrelated changes.
Use delegation only when it helps. Report commands actually executed and unresolved
failures. Do not change tests to manufacture success.

import unittest

from transpose import (
    transpose,

class TransposeTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_empty_string(self):
        text = ""
        expected = ""

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_two_characters_in_a_row(self):
        text = "A1"
        expected = "A
1"

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_two_characters_in_a_column(self):
        text = "A
1"
        expected = "A1"

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_simple(self):
        text = "ABC
123"
        expected = "A1
B2
C3"

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_single_line(self):
        text = "Single line."
        expected = "S
i
n
g
l
e
 
l
i
n
e
."

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_first_line_longer_than_second_line(self):
        text = "The fourth line.
The fifth line."
        expected = "TT
hh
ee

oi

th

 l
li
in
ne
e.
."

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_second_line_longer_than_first_line(self):
        text = "The first line.
The second line."
        expected = "TT
hh
ee
  
fs
ie
rc
so
tn
 d
l 
il
ni
en
.e
 ."

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

 ooi

ei 
snl
tei
 .n

n
e

EMBER
ABUSE
RESIN
TREND"
        expected = "HEART
EMBER
ABUSE
RESIN
TREND"

        self.assertEqual(transpose(text), expected)

    def test_rectangle(self):

# Instructions

Given an input text output it transposed.

Roughly explained, the transpose of a matrix:

```text
ABC
DEF
```

is given by:

```text
AD
BE
CF
```

Rows become columns and columns become rows.
See [transpose][].

If the input has rows of different lengths, this is to be solved as follows:

- Pad to the left with spaces.
- Don't pad to the right.

Therefore, transposing this matrix:

```text
ABC
DE
```

results in:

```text
AD
BE
C
```

And transposing:

```text
AB
DEF
```

results in:

```text
AD
BE
 F
```

In general, all characters from the input should also be present in the transposed output.
That means that if a column in the input text contains only spaces on its bottom-most row(s), the corresponding output row should contain the spaces in its right-most column(s).

[transpose]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpose


Implement the existing API. Use only the standard library. Do not change tests or build manifests. Original tests are available in the workspace.
Run all tests with `python3 -m unittest discover -p '*_test.py'`.

def transpose(text):
    """Transpose ``text``: rows become columns and columns become rows.

    Every input row keeps its characters in their original columns, so shorter
    rows are implicitly padded with spaces on the right.  The padding is not
    written out, though: an output row stops right after the last input row
    that actually reaches that column.  Genuine spaces from the input (even in
    a row consisting only of spaces) are kept, so no character is lost.
    """
    if not text:
        return ""

    lines = text.splitlines()
    width = max(len(line) for line in lines)

    rows = []
    for column in range(width):
        characters = [
            line[column] if column < len(line) else " " for line in lines
        ]
        # Index of the last row with a real character in this column; trailing
        # entries beyond it are padding and are dropped.
        last = max(index for index, line in enumerate(lines) if len(line) > column)
        rows.append("".join(characters[: last + 1]))

    return "\n".join(rows)
